questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of a well-defined hypopigmented patch with loss of sensation on the left forearm. Slit skin smear shows 1 AFB per 100 fields (BI = 1+). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Borderline tuberculoid (BT) leprosy presents with 2-5 hypopigmented patches with reduced sensation. TT leprosy is paucibacillary (BI = 0). A positive BI of 1+ places this in the multibacillary/BT spectrum. BB has bilateral asymmetric 'swiss cheese' lesions.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with painful oral erosions followed by flaccid blisters on the trunk. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows IgG and C3 deposits in intercellular spaces. What is the primary target antigen?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris with mucosal involvement targets Desmoglein 3 (Dsg3). Dsg1 is targeted in pemphigus foliaceus. BP180 is the antigen in bullous pemphigoid. Collagen VII is targeted in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with annular scaly plaques on the inner thigh with central clearing. KOH examination shows septate hyphae and arthrospores. What is the first-line oral treatment?
questions.exp: Terbinafine (allylamine) is the first-line oral treatment for tinea corporis/cruris due to its fungicidal action and shorter treatment duration. It inhibits squalene epoxidase. Griseofulvin is less favored due to longer duration and fungistatic action. Fluconazole is used for candidiasis.

questions.q: A 22-year-old sexually active man presents with a painless genital ulcer that healed spontaneously 3 weeks ago. He now has a diffuse maculopapular rash on palms and soles, generalized lymphadenopathy, and condylomata lata perianally. RPR titre is 1:64. What is the current stage?
questions.exp: Secondary syphilis presents 4-10 weeks after primary chancre resolution with the classic triad: maculopapular palmoplantar rash, generalized lymphadenopathy, and condylomata lata. High RPR titre confirms active disease. Condylomata lata (moist flat warts) distinguish secondary syphilis from condylomata acuminata (HPV).

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with a photosensitive butterfly rash on the face sparing nasolabial folds, arthralgia, and non-scarring alopecia. ANA is 1:320. Which histopathological finding is most characteristic of this condition?
opts: Acanthosis with parakeratosis and neutrophilic infiltrate
Vacuolar degeneration of basal cells with follicular plugging
Subepidermal blister with neutrophil-rich papillary dermal infiltrate
questions.exp: Cutaneous lupus erythematosus shows vacuolar (liquefactive) degeneration of basal keratinocytes, follicular plugging, thickening of basement membrane, and perivascular/periappendageal lymphocytic infiltrate. DIF (lupus band test) shows IgG, IgM, C3 at DEJ in involved skin.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man has a pigmented lesion on the back: asymmetric, irregular borders, multiple colors, 12mm diameter. Biopsy reveals melanoma with Breslow thickness 1.8mm. For which Breslow threshold is sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) indicated?
questions.exp: SLNB is recommended for melanomas with Breslow thickness >1mm. For 0.75-1mm thickness with high-risk features (ulceration, mitotic rate ≥1/mm², lymphovascular invasion), SLNB may also be considered. This patient's 1.8mm thickness clearly meets the >1mm threshold.

questions.q: A 70-year-old diabetic develops severe burning pain in the right thorax, followed by grouped vesicles in a dermatomal distribution not crossing the midline. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. What is the preferred antiviral regimen?
opts: Acyclovir 200mg five times daily for 10 days
Valacyclovir 1000mg three times daily for 7 days
questions.exp: Valacyclovir 1g TID × 7 days is preferred for herpes zoster due to superior bioavailability (54% vs 10-20% for acyclovir), allowing three-times-daily dosing that achieves equivalent antiviral levels with better compliance. Treatment should start within 72 hours of rash onset.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with violaceous, flat-topped polygonal papules on flexor wrists with lacy white streaks on the surface. Biopsy shows saw-tooth rete ridges with band-like lymphocytic infiltrate and eosinophilic cytoid bodies. What are the lacy white streaks called?
questions.exp: Wickham striae are characteristic of lichen planus — lacy white streaks on the surface of violaceous papules, especially on buccal mucosa and glans penis. They represent focal areas of increased granular layer thickness. Histology shows Max-Joseph spaces (clefts at DEJ) and Civatte (colloid) bodies.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man has well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales on elbows and knees. On removing the scale, pinpoint bleeding occurs. What is this sign called?
questions.exp: Auspitz sign (pinpoint capillary bleeding on scale removal) is characteristic of psoriasis, caused by thinning of the suprapapillary plate above dilated capillary loops in elongated dermal papillae. Nikolsky sign is positive in pemphigus. Darier sign is seen in mastocytosis. Koebner is the isomorphic response.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child presents with intense nocturnal pruritus. Burrows are seen in interdigital spaces and wrists. Multiple family members are similarly affected. What is the drug of choice?
questions.exp: Permethrin 5% cream is the drug of choice for scabies. It is applied from neck to toe for 8-12 hours and washed off. Lindane is avoided in children <2 years due to neurotoxicity. Benzyl benzoate causes skin irritation. Ivermectin is not approved for children <15kg and is second-line therapy.

questions.q: A 24-year-old man presents with a painful, soft, non-indurated ulcer with undermined edges and purulent base on the glans penis, along with a tender unilateral inguinal bubo. Gram stain shows Gram-negative coccobacilli in a 'school of fish' pattern. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi) presents with a soft, painful genital ulcer with undermined edges, purulent base, and tender unilateral suppurative bubo. Gram stain shows Gram-negative coccobacilli in 'school of fish' or 'railroad track' pattern. Treatment: azithromycin 1g single dose or ceftriaxone 250mg IM.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman on carbamazepine develops fever and widespread targetoid lesions. Within 48 hours, bullae and epidermal detachment involve >30% BSA. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: TEN is defined by epidermal detachment >30% BSA. SJS involves <10% BSA, and SJS-TEN overlap involves 10-30%. Both are severe cutaneous adverse drug reactions (SCARs), commonly caused by aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, and NSAIDs. SCORTEN score predicts mortality.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man presents with tense blisters on erythematous background on the trunk and thighs without mucosal involvement. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. ELISA confirms antibodies against the NC16A domain of BP180. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid presents in the elderly with tense (not flaccid) blisters on an urticarial/eczematous background, typically without mucosal involvement. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at DEJ (n-serrated pattern). Antibodies target BP180 (collagen XVII, NC16A domain) and BP230. Nikolsky sign is negative.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man has intensely pruritic grouped vesicles on elbows, knees, and scalp with intermittent diarrhea. DIF shows granular IgA deposits at dermal papillary tips. HLA-DQ2 is positive. What is the drug of choice?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhring's disease) is treated with dapsone, which rapidly controls itch and blistering within 24-48 hours. Long-term management requires a strict gluten-free diet, which may eventually allow dapsone dose reduction. G6PD levels must be checked before starting dapsone.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man has generalized erythroderma involving >80% BSA for 6 months. Peripheral blood shows large lymphocytes with cerebriform nuclei >1000/µL, and CD4:CD8 ratio is >10:1. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Sézary syndrome is defined by the triad of erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and circulating Sézary cells (cerebriform lymphocytes) >1000/µL with CD4:CD8 ratio >10:1. It is the leukemic variant of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. MF typically presents with patches and plaques progressing to tumours.

questions.q: A 35-year-old pregnant woman (second trimester) has symmetrical hyperpigmentation on the cheeks in a centrofacial distribution, worsened by sun exposure. What is the safest topical treatment during pregnancy?
questions.exp: Azelaic acid (FDA Category B) is safe in pregnancy for melasma management. Hydroquinone (Category C) should be avoided due to systemic absorption concerns. Tretinoin (Category X) is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. Kojic acid lacks adequate safety data. Sunscreen is the cornerstone of melasma management.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman has depigmented patches on the hands and perioral area. Wood's lamp shows chalky-white fluorescence. Which phototherapy modality has the best evidence for repigmentation in generalized vitiligo?
questions.exp: Narrowband UVB (311-312nm) is the gold standard phototherapy for generalized vitiligo. It is superior to broadband UVB and systemic PUVA, with a better safety profile (less carcinogenic, no phototoxicity risk, usable in children and pregnancy). Excimer laser (308nm) is preferred for localized vitiligo.

questions.q: A 17-year-old with severe nodulocystic acne is started on isotretinoin. What is the primary mechanism of action of isotretinoin in acne?
opts: Sebaceous gland atrophy reducing sebum production by up to 90%
Direct bactericidal action against Cutibacterium acnes
Comedolytic action by normalizing follicular keratinization alone
questions.exp: Isotretinoin's primary mechanism is induction of apoptosis in sebaceous gland cells, causing gland atrophy and up to 90% reduction in sebum production. Secondary effects include normalization of follicular keratinization (comedolytic), reduction in C. acnes colonization (consequent to sebum reduction), and anti-inflammatory effects.

questions.q: A 40-year-old nurse has erythema, vesicles, and pruritus on the dorsum of hands confined to areas under latex gloves. Patch testing shows a positive reaction to thiuram mix at D2 and D4, with no reaction at 20 minutes. What type of hypersensitivity is this?
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis to rubber accelerants (thiuram, carbamates, mercaptobenzothiazole) is a Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction. Positive patch test at 48-96h confirms this. A positive reaction at 20 minutes would indicate Type I (IgE-mediated) latex allergy, which carries a risk of anaphylaxis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man has a painless inguinal swelling divided by Poupart's ligament ('groove sign'). He recalls a self-healing painless genital papule 3 weeks ago. Chlamydia serology complement fixation titre is 1:64. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: LGV is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3. The groove sign (bubo divided by inguinal ligament) is pathognomonic for LGV. Primary LGV shows a transient painless papule/ulcer. CFT titre ≥1:64 or NAAT positivity confirms diagnosis. Treatment: doxycycline 100mg BD for 21 days.

questions.q: A 30-year-old borderline leprosy patient on MDT develops sudden erythema and edema of existing skin lesions, fever, joint pain, and acute neuritis over 2 weeks. No new pustular nodules are seen. What type of lepra reaction is this?
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction occurs in borderline leprosy (BT, BB, BL) due to Type IV delayed hypersensitivity. It presents with erythema and edema of existing lesions plus acute neuritis, without new lesions. ENL (Type 2) presents with fresh tender erythematous nodules/pustules and systemic features in BL/LL. Treatment: prednisolone.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman has tight skin on the hands and forearms proximal to MCP joints, Raynaud's phenomenon, calcinosis, telangiectasia, and dysphagia. ANA shows nucleolar pattern; anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Diffuse cutaneous SSc involves skin proximal to MCP joints (trunk, face, proximal and distal extremities) and is associated with anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibodies and higher risk of interstitial lung disease and renal crisis. Limited cutaneous SSc/CREST has skin involvement distal to elbows/knees with anti-centromere antibodies.

questions.q: A 20-year-old man has multiple hypo- and hyperpigmented macules on the trunk with fine branny scale elicited on stretching. KOH examination shows short hyphae and round spores giving a 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Pityriasis (tinea) versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (and M. globosa). KOH shows short hyphae ('spaghetti') and budding spores ('meatballs'). Hypopigmentation results from azelaic acid production inhibiting melanogenesis. Wood's lamp shows yellow-green fluorescence. Treatment: ketoconazole shampoo, selenium sulfide, or oral fluconazole.

questions.q: A 10-year-old presents with scaling and broken hair shafts (black dots) on the scalp. Wood's lamp examination shows bright green fluorescence. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: Microsporum canis causes ectothrix tinea capitis with bright green fluorescence on Wood's lamp (due to pteridine production). Trichophyton tonsurans causes endothrix infection (black dot tinea capitis) with NO Wood's lamp fluorescence. Epidermophyton does not infect hair. Griseofulvin is the treatment of choice for tinea capitis.

questions.q: A Tzanck smear is prepared from the floor of a blister in a patient with pemphigus vulgaris. What characteristic cells would be identified?
opts: Multinucleated giant cells with intranuclear (Cowdry A) inclusions
Large rounded acantholytic cells with prominent nuclei and perinuclear halo
Neutrophils and eosinophils forming subepidermal pustules
questions.exp: Tzanck smear from pemphigus shows acantholytic (Tzanck) cells — large rounded keratinocytes that have lost their desmosomal attachments, with large nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and a perinuclear halo. In contrast, herpes infections show multinucleated giant cells with Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusions (steel-grey nuclei, nuclear molding).

questions.q: A patient on dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis develops acute onset pallor, fatigue, jaundice, and dark urine. CBC shows Hb 7.2 g/dL and reticulocyte count 12%. Peripheral smear shows Heinz bodies. Which enzyme deficiency predisposes to this complication?
questions.exp: G6PD deficiency predisposes to severe hemolytic anemia with dapsone and other oxidant drugs. G6PD protects RBCs from oxidative damage; its deficiency allows oxidized hemoglobin to denature and form Heinz bodies, leading to intravascular hemolysis. G6PD screening is mandatory before dapsone initiation. Methemoglobinemia is a separate dose-dependent side effect.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man has a pearly, translucent papule with overlying telangiectasia and a central ulcer with rolled pearly edges on the nose, slowly growing over 3 years. What is the most common histological subtype of this tumor?
questions.exp: Nodular BCC is the most common subtype (60-80%), classically presenting as a pearly nodule with telangiectasia that may develop central ulceration ('rodent ulcer'). Morpheaform BCC presents as a scar-like plaque with ill-defined borders and carries the worst prognosis. Superficial BCC is commonest on the trunk.

questions.q: A neonate develops widespread blistering after minimal birth trauma. Electron microscopy of the skin biopsy shows the cleavage plane within the lamina lucida of the basement membrane zone. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: The level of skin cleavage defines EB subtypes: EBS — intraepidermal (suprabasal or basal layer), keratin 5/14 mutations; JEB — within lamina lucida, laminin 332 or collagen XVII mutations; DEB — below lamina densa (sublamina densa), collagen VII mutations. JEB (Herlitz type) carries a poor prognosis with laryngeal and GI involvement.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with widespread wheals and angioedema for 8 weeks. Individual lesions last <24 hours and resolve without scarring. Despite extensive investigation, no triggering factor is identified. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) is defined by urticarial wheals, angioedema, or both occurring >6 weeks without a specific identifiable trigger. First-line treatment is second-generation non-sedating H1 antihistamines. Omalizumab (anti-IgE) is approved for antihistamine-refractory CSU. Urticarial vasculitis lesions last >24h and leave bruising.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman has heliotrope periorbital discoloration, Gottron's papules over MCP/PIP joints, V-sign and shawl sign, proximal muscle weakness, elevated CK, and dyspnea from interstitial lung disease. Which autoantibody is most associated with dermatomyositis combined with ILD?
questions.exp: Anti-Jo-1 (anti-aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase) is associated with antisynthetase syndrome: inflammatory myopathy (DM/PM) + ILD + arthritis + mechanic's hands + Raynaud's. Anti-Mi-2 is the most specific antibody for classic dermatomyositis but is associated with better prognosis and less ILD. Anti-MDA5 is associated with amyopathic DM and severe ILD.
